questions.question: What does the price of a product tell us?
options: How good the product is.
How much we need to pay for it.
How long the product will last.
What material it is made of.
questions.explanation: Price tells us how much money we have to pay, not necessarily how good the product is.

questions.question: A more expensive product is always better quality than a cheaper one.
questions.explanation: A higher price can reflect brand, packaging, or advertising - not just better quality.

questions.question: What does quality mean when talking about a product?
options: How expensive it is.
How colorful the packaging is.
How well it works and how long it lasts.
Where it was made.
questions.explanation: Quality describes how well a product functions and how durable it is over time.

questions.question: Sometimes a higher price is caused by the brand name, not by better materials.
questions.explanation: Well-known brands often charge more due to marketing and reputation, not always superior quality.

questions.question: Chrumko is choosing a pencil. One has a fancy branded package and costs more. A simpler one next to it costs less and writes just as well. Which is the wiser choice?
options: Always the branded one, because it is more expensive and therefore better.
The cheaper one, since it performs the same and saves money.
Neither - he should not buy pencils at all.
The branded one, because the nice packaging lasts longer.
questions.explanation: If both products perform the same, the cheaper one is the smarter buy.

questions.question: Decide what each factor mainly affects.

dragTargets.label: Raises price without improving the product

questions.explanation: Better materials improve the product itself; brand and packaging mostly increase the price.

questions.question: Put these steps in the right order for choosing between two similar products.
orderItems: Try or compare how they work
Think about whether the price difference is worth it
Choose the one with better value
questions.explanation: Smart shopping means comparing both function and price before deciding.

questions.question: Chrumko finds two pens that write exactly the same, but one has a fancier package and costs more.
options: He should buy the fancier one because higher price always means better quality.
He should buy the cheaper one, since it performs identically and costs less.
He should buy both to compare over time.
Price differences never matter when items work the same.
questions.explanation: If both products perform the same, the cheaper one is the smarter buy.

questions.question: One of these statements is wrong. Find it.
options: A more expensive product is always better quality than a cheaper one.
Quality describes how well a product functions and how durable it is.
A higher price can sometimes come from the brand name rather than better materials.
questions.explanation: A more expensive product is NOT always better quality - price can reflect brand, packaging, or advertising instead.

questions.question: Why can two very similar products have completely different prices?
options: Because more expensive ones are always newer.
Because the shop owner sets prices randomly each morning.
Because cheaper products are always worse.
Because price depends on material, brand, packaging, and where it is sold.
questions.explanation: Many factors influence price: production method, brand, packaging size, and the shop itself.

questions.question: The same product can cost different amounts in different shops.
questions.explanation: Different shops have different costs and pricing strategies for the same item.

questions.question: What is usually the best reason to choose a more expensive product over a cheaper one?
options: It has a nicer colour.
The shop put it on a higher shelf.
It is made of better materials and will last longer.
It costs more, so it must be better.
questions.explanation: A higher price is only justified when the product genuinely offers better durability or function.

questions.question: Chrumko finds two identical notebooks - same page count, same use - but one costs more because of its cover design. The cheaper one is a reasonable choice.
questions.explanation: If the only difference is appearance and not function, the cheaper option is often wiser.

questions.question: Match each reason for a price difference to its correct description.
questions.explanation: Price differences can come from brand, materials, or simply the amount you get.

questions.question: Chrumko sees a notebook with a fancy cover for €3 and a plain notebook for €1.50. Both have the same number of pages. What should he think about first?
options: Whether the price difference is worth it for just a different cover.
Which one his friends would choose.
He must always buy the cheaper one no matter what.
He must always buy the more expensive one to be safe.
questions.explanation: It is wise to evaluate whether a price difference reflects a real benefit to you.

questions.question: Sort each factor into what it actually affects.
questions.explanation: Packaging and brand raise the price; durable materials raise both price and quality.

questions.question: Chrumko finds two identical bags of the same brand and material in different shops - one costs more than the other.
options: He should always buy from the first shop he visited.
He should buy from the cheaper shop, since it's the exact same product.
The more expensive one must be better because it costs more.
Price never differs between shops for the same item.
questions.explanation: The same product can cost different amounts in different shops - buying from the cheaper shop for an identical item is the smarter choice.

questions.question: One of these statements is wrong. Find it.
options: The same product can cost different amounts in different shops.
A higher price is only justified when the product genuinely offers better durability or function.
Cheaper products are always worse in every single case.
questions.explanation: Cheaper products are not always worse - many price differences come from brand, packaging, or shop location rather than quality.

questions.question: What does it mean to get a good deal?
options: Always buying the cheapest product available.
Buying as many items as possible at once.
Buying something that works well and lasts long for a fair price.
Buying things only during sales.
questions.explanation: A good deal means the product serves its purpose well and the price matches what it offers.

questions.question: A cheap product that breaks quickly is always a good deal because it cost less.
questions.explanation: If a cheap product breaks quickly, you may need to replace it sooner, making it more expensive in the long run.

questions.question: Put the steps in order for deciding if something is a good deal.
orderItems: Decide if the price matches what you get
questions.explanation: A good deal requires comparing price, quality, and usefulness before buying.

questions.question: When can a more expensive product actually be the better deal?
options: When it has a shinier package.
When you use it every day and it lasts much longer than the cheap version.
When the shop owner says it is better.
When it is the most expensive item in the shop.
questions.explanation: Paying more for something durable that you use daily can cost less overall than replacing a cheap version repeatedly.

questions.question: Chrumko buys a cheap water bottle that cracks after a week. He then must buy another one. This was not a good deal.
questions.explanation: A cheap product that needs replacing quickly often costs more in total than a better-quality one bought once.

questions.question: Decide if each purchase sounds like a good deal or a bad deal.
dragLabels: Sturdy bag used daily for 2 years
Cheap toy that breaks after one day
Simple pen that writes perfectly all year

dragTargets.label: Good deal
correctItems: Sturdy bag used daily for 2 years
Simple pen that writes perfectly all year

dragTargets.label: Bad deal
correctItems: Cheap toy that breaks after one day

questions.explanation: A good deal means the product lasts and serves its purpose well for its price.

questions.question: Chrumko wants a water bottle for school. He sees a thin cheap one and a sturdier one that costs a bit more. What is the smartest question to ask himself?
options: Which one looks more fun?
Which one will I use every day and which will last longer?
Which one is the most popular?
Which one does my friend have?
questions.explanation: For daily-use items, durability and long-term value are the most important factors.

questions.question: Chrumko buys the cheapest water bottle he can find, and it cracks after just one week, forcing him to buy another.
options: This was a good deal since he paid the least amount possible.
This was not a good deal, since he ended up needing to buy another one quickly.
Cheap products always last the longest.
The price alone tells you everything about how good a deal is.
questions.explanation: A cheap product that needs replacing quickly often costs more in total than a better-quality one bought once - this was not a good deal.

questions.question: One of these statements is wrong. Find it.
options: A good deal means the product works well, lasts long, and its price matches what it offers.
Paying more for something durable that you use daily can cost less overall than replacing a cheap version repeatedly.
A cheap product that breaks quickly is always a good deal because it cost less.
questions.explanation: A cheap product that breaks quickly is NOT always a good deal - you may need to replace it sooner, making it more expensive in the long run.

questions.question: Why is it useful to compare prices before buying something?
options: To make shopping trips longer and more fun.
Because cheaper products are always of worse quality.
To confuse the shopkeeper.
Because the same product can cost less in a different shop.
questions.explanation: Comparing prices helps you find the same product at a better price, saving money.

questions.question: It is worth comparing prices even for small purchases, because small savings add up over time.
questions.explanation: Even small price differences accumulate into significant savings when shopping regularly.

questions.question: Chrumko finds the same coloured pencils in two shops - one sells them for €4, the other for €2.80. What should he do?
options: Buy from the first shop because he was there first.
Buy from the second shop to get the same product for less money.
Not buy pencils at all because prices are different.
Buy one pack from each shop.
questions.explanation: Buying the same product at a lower price is a smart financial decision.

questions.question: If two packs of pencils are identical in content but different in price, the more expensive one is the better deal.
questions.explanation: If the content is identical, the cheaper pack gives the same value for less money.

questions.question: Match each shopping situation to the smart action.
matchLeft: Two products, same shop, same use
Product you have never seen before
matchRight: Choose the one with better price-to-quality ratio
questions.explanation: Smart shopping means adjusting your approach depending on the situation.

questions.question: Chrumko buys coloured pencils in the nearest shop without checking elsewhere. Later his friend shows him the same pack costs much less online. What did Chrumko miss?
options: The chance to save money by comparing prices first.
Nothing - speed is always worth paying for.
He made the right choice because online shopping is risky.
He should have bought two packs to get a discount.
questions.explanation: Price comparison is a simple habit that can save money with little extra effort.

questions.question: Chrumko wants to buy coloured pencils and sees them at the first shop he visits without checking anywhere else.
options: He should buy immediately without comparing, since comparing wastes time.
He should check if the same product costs less somewhere else before buying.
The first shop he visits is always the cheapest.
Comparing prices only matters for very expensive purchases.
questions.explanation: It is worth comparing prices even for small purchases, since the same product can cost less in a different shop.

questions.question: One of these statements is wrong. Find it.
options: The same product can cost less in a different shop.
It is worth comparing prices even for small purchases, because small savings add up over time.
If two packs of pencils are identical in content but different in price, the more expensive one is always the better deal.
questions.explanation: If the content is identical, the CHEAPER pack gives the same value for less money, not the more expensive one.

questions.question: What is a unit price?
options: The price of the most expensive item in the shop.
The total price you pay at the checkout.
The price for one piece, one litre, or one gram of a product.
The price before a discount is applied.
questions.explanation: Unit price tells you the cost per single unit of measurement, making it easy to compare packages.

questions.question: A bigger package always costs more in total but can be cheaper per unit.
questions.explanation: Larger packages often have a lower unit price even if their total price is higher.

questions.question: Chrumko sees two water bottles: a 0.5 L bottle for €0.60 and a 1.5 L bottle for €1.20. Which is cheaper per litre?
options: The 0.5 L bottle, because it costs less in total.
The 1.5 L bottle, because it costs less per litre.
They cost the same per litre.
It is impossible to compare them.
questions.explanation: 0.5 L = €1.20/L; 1.5 L = €0.80/L - the large bottle is cheaper per litre.

questions.question: If Chrumko only needs a small amount of something, the larger package is always the better choice.
questions.explanation: A lower unit price is only an advantage if you will actually use the larger quantity.

questions.question: Put the steps for calculating which package is better value in order.
orderItems: Note the total price and the amount of each package
Divide the price by the amount to get the unit price
Choose the one with the lower unit price (if you need that amount)
questions.explanation: Calculating unit price lets you compare packages of different sizes fairly.

questions.question: Chrumko sees two packs of juice: a small pack (200 ml) for €0.50 and a large pack (1000 ml) for €1.80. Sort the facts.
dragLabels: Better if he only wants a little

dragTargets.label: Small pack (200 ml / €0.50)
correctItems: Better if he only wants a little

questions.explanation: Small pack: €0.25/100 ml. Large pack: €0.18/100 ml. Large is cheaper per unit, but small is better if little is needed.

questions.question: Chrumko's mum shows him that two small bottles of water together cost more than one big bottle with the same total volume. What is the lesson?
options: Big bottles are always the right choice.
The total price on the label is not always enough - comparing the unit price shows the real value.
Small bottles are always worse quality.
He should only ever buy big packages from now on.
questions.explanation: Unit price comparison reveals true value that the label price alone does not show.

questions.question: Chrumko only needs a small amount of juice for one trip, but sees a giant bottle with a much lower price per litre.
options: He should always buy the giant bottle since a lower unit price is always better regardless of need.
He should think about whether he'll actually use that much, since a lower unit price only helps if you need the larger quantity.
Unit price never matters for small trips.
The giant bottle is always cheaper in total than the small one.
questions.explanation: A lower unit price is only an advantage if you will actually use the larger quantity - for a single trip, the smaller pack may make more sense.

questions.question: One of these statements is wrong. Find it.
options: Unit price is the price for one piece, one litre, or one gram of a product.
A bigger package always costs more in total but can be cheaper per unit.
If Chrumko only needs a small amount of something, the larger package is always the better choice.
questions.explanation: The larger package is NOT always the better choice - a lower unit price only helps if you will actually use that larger quantity.
